title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?

keyTerms.d: The line was not the mere posture of homage: Israelites could and did bow low before a king as well as before God — 1 Chronicles 29:20 uses a single verb of prostration for both the LORD and King David in the same breath. What Jewish monotheism guarded jealously for God was not the posture of homage but the substance of worship — sacrifice, invocation, prayer.

In Revelation, when John falls down to worship the angel who has shown him the vision, the angel recoils — twice: “You must not do that!… Worship God.” (Revelation 19:10; 22:9). Even the highest created messenger refuses the worship due God alone. That refusal tells us precisely what the earliest Christians thought they were — and were not — free to do.

An Aramaic prayer, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22), preserved untranslated in Paul’s Greek — a fossil of devotion in the original language of the Palestinian church, carrying us behind Paul’s Greek to the first Aramaic-speaking believers in Jerusalem in the 30s. It is not the homage due a vice-regent; it is an invocation, calling on the risen Lord to come.

Paul can define the whole church, in a single phrase, as “all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:2), taking up the Scriptures’ own idiom for invoking YHWH by name (Joel 2:32; Romans 10:13).

Larry Hurtado’s term for a pattern of devotion — worship offered to Jesus together with God the Father — which he concluded emerged “amazingly early,” within the first two decades of the movement, among Jews who would have regarded worshipping any creature as blasphemy. They held, in one breath, that God is one and that the crucified Jesus was to be worshipped. “Binitarian” describes the shape of the earliest devotion, not a two-person God; the same faith confesses one God, Father, Son and Spirit.

The Jewish principle that “a man’s agent is as the man himself”: an ambassador is honoured, obeyed, even received as though he were the king — without being the king. But agency has a ceiling: no shaliach in Jewish thought ever received the cultic devotion — the prayer, the invocation, the hymn offered to a god — that the sources give Jesus. Agency conferred authority; it never conferred that adoration.

The technical creedal vocabulary and systematic formulation (Nicaea’s “one essence,” Chalcedon’s “two natures”) came later, as the church’s articulation of what it was already doing. That is not to say the worship of Jesus, or his deity, was a later human invention: the devotion — prayer to Jesus, the hymn sung of him, invocation of his name — is present from the earliest layers we can reach.

Richard Bauckham’s thesis that the New Testament writers deliberately include Jesus within the unique divine identity of the one God. It is influential but genuinely contested: Dunn, and from another angle James F. McGrath, question how sharply that boundary can be drawn, and Hurtado preferred to frame the data as devotional practice. The early-and-high-devotion datum is firm; this framing of it is a powerful but disputed interpretation.

derive.q: 1 Chronicles 29:20 uses one verb of prostration for both the LORD and King David — so the line Judaism guarded was…?
derive.ans: the substance of worship, not the posture of homage
derive.why: Bowing, kneeling, honouring: these could be offered to prophets, kings, and angels without blasphemy. What Jewish monotheism guarded jealously for God was not the posture of homage but the substance of worship — sacrifice, invocation, prayer.

derive.q: In Revelation an angel twice refuses worship — “You must not do that!… Worship God” — so even the highest created messenger…?
derive.ans: may not receive the worship due God alone
derive.why: That refusal is the control case: it tells us precisely what the earliest Christians thought they were — and were not — free to do. And it makes what they did with Jesus all the more startling.

derive.q: In the same book the whole created order sings to “him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb” the same blessing and honour and glory — so the Lamb…?
derive.why: The elders fall down in worship (Revelation 5:13–14) — in the very book whose angel twice refuses that worship for himself. Hebrews goes further still: God commands the worship — “Let all God’s angels worship him” (Hebrews 1:6) — in words whose Old Testament source directs that worship to the LORD.

derive.q: An Aramaic prayer to the risen Lord, left untranslated in a Greek letter written around the year 55 — so it reaches…?
derive.ans: behind Paul to the first Aramaic-speaking believers
derive.why: Marana tha is a fossil of devotion in the original language of the Palestinian church, carrying us behind Paul’s Greek to the first Aramaic-speaking believers in Jerusalem in the 30s. The consonants can also be divided maran atha, “our Lord has come,” but the imperative prayer is the standard reading, matched by Revelation 22:20.

derive.q: A pagan governor, around AD 112, reports Christians singing “a hymn to Christ, as to a god” — so his testimony shows…?
derive.ans: the practice entrenched — not its origin
derive.why: It is hostile testimony that, by the early second century, worshipping Jesus was already the settled, customary practice of the churches Pliny encountered. His testimony corroborates the entrenchment of the practice, while the New Testament evidence establishes its earlier origin. The force of quasi deo is disputed; Sherwin-White argues quasi here means simply “as,” not “as if.”

derive.q: Grant all of it: the first Christians worshipped Jesus, and early. Does that, by itself, prove Jesus is God?
derive.ans: no — it shows the worship was early, not that it was warranted
derive.why: It does not, by itself, prove that the worship was warranted — that Jesus is in fact God, and rightly adored. That is the separate work of his resurrection and of his own words and deeds. Nor does it hand us the developed metaphysics of the fourth-century councils, which the honest case concedes came later.

honestState.p1: The early-and-high-devotion datum is firm. Hurtado devoted a major study to exactly this question and concluded that the pattern of devotion to Jesus together with God the Father emerged “amazingly early,” within the first two decades. Dunn presses the most cautious of the major treatments — he questions how much weight the category “worship” will bear in the earliest texts, and answers that worship was characteristically offered to God through Jesus rather than to Jesus as such — yet grants that the devotion is real and early; his caution is a minority position relative to Hurtado and Bauckham. Even Ehrman rejects the crude “Constantine invented it” story and grants that devotion to Jesus began strikingly early.
honestState.fairness: Several supports are debated, and the case says so. The Philippians hymn is widely regarded as pre-Pauline, but Gordon Fee argues Paul composed it himself — the worship it expresses stands either way. The force of Pliny’s quasi deo is disputed. Matthew’s verb proskyneō can by itself mean no more than homage, so the force of that scene lies in Matthew’s frame, not the word. The church’s formal vocabulary — the fourth-century language of “one essence” — genuinely did develop later. And Bauckham’s “divine identity” framing is influential but genuinely contested: Dunn, and from another angle James F. McGrath, question how sharply that boundary can be drawn, and Hurtado preferred to frame the data as devotional practice.
honestState.verdict: What the evidence establishes is enough to dissolve the “slow development” myth. The first Christians — Jewish monotheists who would die before bowing to an idol — prayed to Jesus, sang of him, called on his name, and worshipped him where they refused to worship even an angel; and they did so from the earliest years of the movement, not after centuries of drift. They held, in one breath, that God is one and that the crucified Jesus was to be worshipped. That is worship, offered at the start — and worship, in a Jew, is a confession about who God is. It does not by itself prove the worship warranted; that case is argued from Scripture and the resurrection. We hold that this worship is rightly placed — that the one they prayed to is, as Nicaea confessed, true God from true God, one God with the Father and the Spirit.

order: Jewish monotheism reserved the substance of worship — not the posture of homage — for the one God alone.
The earliest Christians gave exactly that worship to Jesus, in the earliest layer we can reach.
Therefore the first Christians worshipped Jesus, and did so from the start — not after centuries of drift.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and exactly where the line falls.
cards.a: Jewish monotheism reserved for the one God alone not the posture of homage — Israelites bowed before kings too (1 Chronicles 29:20 uses one verb for both) — but the substance of cultic worship: sacrifice, invocation, prayer, the hymn to a god. Even an angel refuses it (“Worship God,” Revelation 19:10; 22:9).

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and what kind of claim it is.
cards.a: The earliest Christians gave exactly that worship to Jesus, and it was early, not a slow climb. The claim is about the practice, not the vocabulary: the words the church later coined to explain the devotion came slowly; the devotion itself was there at the beginning.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the first Christians worshipped Jesus from the start, not after centuries of drift — and worship, in a Jew, is a confession about who God is. It does not by itself prove the worship was warranted — that Jesus is in fact God — which is the separate work of the resurrection and of his own words and deeds; nor does it hand us the fourth-century councils’ metaphysics.

cards.q: Why does the angel’s refusal in Revelation matter so much?
cards.a: It is the control case. Even the highest created messenger refuses the worship due God alone, which tells us precisely what the earliest Christians thought they were — and were not — free to do. And in the same book the Lamb receives the same blessing and honour and glory as the one on the throne: the Lamb receives what the angel forbids.

cards.q: What did the first believers actually DO that counts as worship, not homage?
cards.a: They prayed to him (Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!”; Stephen’s “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit”), called on his name in the Scriptures’ own idiom for invoking YHWH (1 Corinthians 1:2; Joel 2:32), sang of him — and, as a hostile outsider reported by around AD 112, to him — and worshipped him where they refused to worship an angel.

cards.q: Why is Marana tha the strongest single piece of evidence for an EARLY date?
cards.a: Because it is Aramaic — a fossil of devotion in the original language of the Palestinian church, preserved untranslated in Paul’s Greek. It carries us behind Paul to the first Aramaic-speaking believers in Jerusalem in the 30s. The most explosive evidence is also the earliest.

cards.q: What does the hostile outsider’s report add — and what is its limit?
cards.a: Hostile testimony that by the early second century worshipping Jesus was already the settled, customary practice of the churches he encountered: “a hymn to Christ, as to a god.” Limit: it corroborates the entrenchment of the practice, while the New Testament evidence establishes its earlier origin; and the force of quasi deo is disputed.

cards.q: Matthew’s verb for “worship” can mean mere homage — so where does the force of the scene lie?
cards.a: In the frame, not the word. The same Gospel that has Jesus refuse Satan’s demand for worship by quoting “him only shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10) closes with the risen Jesus receiving it from his disciples and answering, not with the angel’s refusal, but with a claim to all authority in heaven and on earth. The candour of “some doubted” shows Matthew is not concealing the difficulty.

cards.q: “He was only God’s supreme agent” — where exactly does agency hit its ceiling?
cards.a: At the altar. An emissary can bear the sender’s name and authority, and the reading should be met on its merits, not caricatured. But no shaliach in Jewish thought ever received the cultic devotion — the prayer, the invocation, the hymn offered to a god — that the sources give Jesus. Even supposing God’s name and functions could be entrusted to an agent, the worship itself could not be.

cards.q: “Early reverence grew into full worship over time” — what is conceded, and what refused?
cards.a: Conceded: the church’s formal vocabulary — the fourth-century language of “one essence” — genuinely developed later. Refused: that the worship itself did. The refinement was in how the church explained the worship of Jesus, never in whether it offered it. On Hurtado’s reading (debated — Dunn is more cautious), that is why the worship of Jesus was a startling “mutation” within Jewish monotheism rather than an unremarkable promotion.

cards.q: “The strongest worship scenes are in the latest books” — why does that not rescue a slow development?
cards.a: Because the case rests its weight on the earliest material, not the latest: a pre-Pauline Aramaic prayer from the Jerusalem church of the 30s, a hymn widely regarded as older than the letter that carries it, and Paul’s undisputed letters of the 50s defining the church as those who “call upon the name” of Jesus. Revelation and John make the worship vivid; they did not invent it.

cards.q: Does the Son of Man in the Similitudes of Enoch break the line?
cards.a: It is the nearest thing to an exception, and should be named. But the figure’s inclusion is partial and equivocal: it lies in the future, at the last judgment, with no share in creating the world. What the text describes is end-time homage before God’s appointed judge, joined to praise of the Lord of Spirits — not a community’s present prayer, invocation and hymn. Its date is also disputed.

obj.q: Jesus was revered as a great teacher. Only slowly, over generations of drift into the Greek world, was he inflated into a god to be worshipped — Constantine’s council finally settled it.
obj.model: It runs aground on the dates. The worship of Jesus is in the earliest sources we possess, centuries before Nicaea: an Aramaic prayer to the risen Jesus from the first Judean church (Marana tha), a hymn sung of him that is widely regarded as pre-Pauline, and — from a hostile outsider — Pliny’s report (c. 112) that Christians sang “a hymn to Christ, as to a god.” Larry Hurtado concluded that this devotion emerged “amazingly early,” within the first two decades, among Jews who would have regarded worshipping any creature as blasphemy. Nicaea did not decide whether to worship Jesus; that was long settled. It excluded Arius, who said the Son was a created being — a debate within a church already worshipping him.

obj.q: “A man’s agent is as the man himself.” An ambassador is honoured and received as though he were the king, without being the king. Jesus is God’s supreme agent — given honour, even a kind of worship, as the perfect representative.
obj.model: Grant the language of sending: in the Hebrew Bible an emissary can bear the sender’s name and authority, and the reading should be met on its merits, not caricatured. But agency has a ceiling, and the worship evidence crashes through it. No shaliach in Jewish thought ever received the cultic devotion — the prayer, the invocation, the hymn offered to a god — that the sources give Jesus. Agency conferred authority; it never conferred that adoration. That is exactly why the angel in Revelation, himself God’s messenger and agent, refuses the very worship the Lamb accepts. Nor is Dunn’s “through Jesus” pattern the whole of it: Paul pleads directly with the Lord whose power he calls “the power of Christ” (2 Corinthians 12:8–9), Stephen commits his spirit to him (Acts 7:59), and the church is defined as those who call upon his name (1 Corinthians 1:2). Even supposing the framework could account for the titles, it still breaks at the altar. So the agency reading does not hold.

obj.q: Granted, devotion to Jesus began early. But early reverence is not yet the later dogma: an initial “exaltation” devotion grew, over time and reflection, into the full worship of Jesus as God in the same sense as the Father.
obj.model: The concession comes first, because part of this is true: the church’s formal vocabulary for what it was doing — the fourth-century language of “one essence” — genuinely did develop later. But the datum is not the vocabulary; it is the practice, and the practice is in the earliest layer we can reach. Marana tha, the Philippians hymn, the pattern Hurtado documents: these are not the top of a slow climb. They are the bedrock. The refinement was in how the church explained the worship of Jesus, never in whether it offered it. And the disagreement is not really about dates — Ehrman himself finds a pre-existent Christ in material older than Paul’s letters — but about what kind of being the earliest Christians took Jesus to be. Whatever room Judaism had for exalted intermediaries, its angels characteristically refuse worship, while the earliest Christians were praying to Jesus and singing hymns about him within the first two decades. That is exactly why Hurtado calls the worship of Jesus a startling “mutation” rather than an unremarkable promotion.

obj.q: Your texts often just say people “bowed” or “fell down” before Jesus. Israelites bowed before kings too — the same gesture. Posture proves nothing about deity.
obj.model: Correct — and the case concedes it in as many words: the posture of homage was never the reserved line (1 Chronicles 29:20 uses one verb of prostration for both the LORD and King David). That is precisely why the load-bearing evidence is not the posture-word at all, but the substance of worship — the things that could never be given to a king: an Aramaic prayer to the risen Jesus, invocation of his name, the hymn sung “to Christ, as to a god,” and the worship an angel refuses. Where the argument leans on Matthew’s proskyneō, its force comes from the frame — Jesus refuses Satan’s worship, then receives his disciples’ and claims all authority — not from the word.

unseen.q: Texts are only words, copied by believers who could shape them. Is there any physical evidence — not just what Christian writings say — that ordinary Christians actually treated Jesus as God?
unseen.model: The evidence does reach beyond what the texts say. The earliest Christian copyists wrote a small set of sacred words in a special abbreviated form, and the earliest and most consistent of them are the words for God and Lord and the names Jesus and Christ — a practice Larry Hurtado read as one more expression of devotion to Jesus together with God the Father. A mosaic in a prayer hall at Kefar ‘Othnay, near Megiddo, records that a woman named Akeptous offered the table “to God Jesus Christ” as a memorial; the excavators date it to the third century, though the date is debated. And on the Palatine Hill in Rome, scratched into a plaster wall around AD 200, a Roman hand drew a man lifting his hand toward a crucified figure with a donkey’s head and wrote beneath it, “Alexamenos worships his god” — a jeer at a Christian for adoring a crucified man. These are later than the earliest texts, so they corroborate the practice rather than date its beginning; the origin is shown by the earliest layer itself, Marana tha and the hymn.
